extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the algebraic-geometry criteria and equivalent characterizations appearing in the chapter: local/global criteria for flatness, fibral flatness statements, consequences of flatness for cohomology and numerical invariants, and equivalent/alternate definitions of smooth and étale morphisms (including formal lifting characterizations and generic-smoothness results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local (slicing) criterion for flatness (Theorem 24.6.2 / Exercise 24.6.F)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the local criterion for flatness to test flatness after slicing by an element f: e.g., if M is a B-module generated over A and multiplication by f is injective on M/nM for maximal ideals n, then under the hypotheses of the local criterion one can deduce flatness properties of M/fM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in exercises: if M is B-flat then M/fM is also B-flat (hint: use Theorem 24.6.2). The Noetherian hypotheses in Exercise 24.6.F can be removed (Remark 24.6.7): if (B,n)→(A,m) is a flat local homomorphism and A is essentially finitely presented over B and f∈A is a nonzero-divisor in B/mB, then A/f is flat over B (see Stacks tag 046Z). This is often used by induction / slicing arguments to deduce flatness on quotients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative effective Cartier divisor and flatness
rubrics_metrics.description: A relative effective Cartier divisor is defined as a locally principal subscheme of X that is an effective Cartier divisor on every fiber of π: X→Y; if π is flat then any relative effective Cartier divisor is flat over Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation of Exercise 24.6.F. In particular, for π flat, locally principal subschemes which are Cartier on fibers remain flat over the base; useful for describing divisors in families and for applications (see Exercise 28.3.F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibral flatness (easy base-change lemma, Exercise 24.6.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a commutative diagram X -τ→ Z -ρ→ Y with π:X→Y and a quasi-coherent sheaf F on X and points p∈X, q=π(p)∈Z, r=τ(p)∈Y: if ρ is flat at q and F is π-flat at p then F is τ-flat at p, and the restriction F|r is πr-flat at p (where πr is the restriction of π to the fiber over r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a straightforward base-change-type observation used to propagate flatness along compositions when one map is flat; useful as a building block in fibral flatness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibral Flatness Theorem (24.6.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose X→Y→Z is a commuting diagram, F is a finitely presented quasi-coherent sheaf on X, and p∈X (with q=π(p) and r=τ(p)); assume either X,Y are locally Noetherian or ρ and τ are locally of finite presentation. Then the following are equivalent: (a) F is τ-flat at p and F|r is πr-flat at p; (b) ρ is flat at q and F is π-flat at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem gives an equivalence relating flatness of the base-change map ρ and flatness of F over the intermediate base; it is a principal tool to reduce flatness questions to the Noetherian case and then to commutative-algebra problems. The proof strategy is: reduce to affine case, reduce to Noetherian case (EGA), and solve the commutative algebra problem (EGA references given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler characteristic is locally constant in flat projective families (Theorem 24.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π:X→Y is projective with Y locally Noetherian and F is a coherent sheaf on X flat over Y, then the Euler characteristic χ(X_q, F|_{X_q}) = Σ(-1)^i dim H^i(X_q, F|_{X_q}) is a locally constant function of q∈Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline: reduce to X = P^n_B, twist so higher cohomology vanishes, use the Čech complex whose terms are flat, tack on Γ(π_*F(m)) at the front to get an exact complex of flat modules, then apply that in such a sequence if all but first terms are flat the first is flat as well (Exercise 24.3.G), so pushforwards are locally free and their ranks (h^0 etc.) are locally constant. Noetherian hypothesis ensures coherence of π_*F(m). Converses appear in Exercise 24.7.A(b)–(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert polynomial and numerical invariants are locally constant in flat projective families (Corollary 24.7.2 / 24.7.B / 24.7.C / 24.7.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 24.7.1 (flat coherent sheaf on a projective morphism), the Hilbert polynomial of the restriction F|_{X_q} is locally constant on Y; for projective flat families the degree, fiber dimension, and arithmetic genus of fibers are locally constant; for line bundles on flat projective families of curves the degree on fibers is locally constant; intersection numbers in flat projective families are locally constant under suitable hypotheses (Exercise 24.7.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are concrete corollaries used to control numerical invariants in families. The degree result for line bundles follows because χ(L|_{X_q}) is constant and degree is expressible via Euler characteristics. The intersection-number statement is a starred exercise relying on flatness and support-dimension hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic equivalence of line bundles (Definition 24.7.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two line bundles L1 and L2 on a k-variety X are algebraically equivalent if there exists a connected k-variety Y with two k-points q1 and q2 and a line bundle L on X×Y whose restrictions to the fibers over q1 and q2 are isomorphic to L1 and L2 respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the definition used to define Pic^0 and the Néron–Severi group Pic(X)/Pic^0(X). The text notes standard properties (equivalence relation, subgroup of Pic X consisting of line bundles algebraically equivalent to O, torsion properties, and references to SGA6 and Lazarsfeld).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence characterizations of smooth morphisms (Theorem 25.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a morphism π:X→Y the following are equivalent: (i) π is smooth of relative dimension n (Definition 12.6.2); (ii) π is locally finitely presented and flat of relative dimension n and Ω_{π} is locally free of rank n; (iii) π is locally finitely presented and flat and the fibers are smooth k-schemes of pure dimension n; (iv) π is locally finitely presented and flat and the geometric fibers are smooth k-schemes of pure dimension n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem supplies the preferred alternate definitions of smoothness used throughout: one may check local finite presentation + flatness + local freeness of relative differentials, or check flatness and smoothness of fibers (or geometric fibers). The proof proceeds by reducing to affine/Noetherian situations, using Jacobian criteria on fibers and Nakayama-type arguments to lift generators. Exercises 25.2.A, 25.2.H, and 25.2.I give auxiliary steps used in the implication chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizations of étale morphisms (Exercises 25.2.B and 25.2.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π is étale iff it is locally of finite presentation, flat, and Ω_π = 0. Equivalently (Exercise 25.2.C), π is étale iff it is smooth and unramified; iff it is locally finitely presented, flat, and unramified; iff for each q∈Y the fiber π^{-1}(q) is a disjoint union of Specs of finite separable extensions of κ(q); iff for each geometric point q the fiber is a disjoint union of copies of q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These equivalent characterizations let one check étaleness via infinitesimal criteria (Ω_π=0), via being smooth of relative dimension 0, or via fiber shape conditions (finite separable field extensions). Exercise 25.2.C lists the equivalences explicitly and demonstrates practical tests (including fiberwise descriptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formally smooth / formally unramified / formally étale (infinitesimal lifting property, 25.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π:X→Y is formally smooth (resp. formally étale, formally unramified) if for every affine scheme Z and every closed immersion Z_0→Z defined by a nilpotent ideal, the map Hom_Y(Z,X)→Hom_Y(Z_0,X) is surjective (resp. bijective, injective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Grothendieck (EGA) infinitesimal lifting formulation; EGA then defines smooth/unramified/étale as formally smooth/unramified/étale plus locally finite presentation. The text notes equivalence with other definitions (references to EGA/Stacks tags) and that this viewpoint is useful for certain exactness properties and cotangent-complex interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient local criteria for smoothness (Exercises 25.2.D, 25.2.F, 25.2.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful sufficient checks: (a) If π is étale at a preimage p of a regular point q whose local ring has dimension n, then p is regular of same dimension (25.2.D). (b) If π:X→Y with X,Y smooth and fibers of π are all smooth of dimension m−n then π is smooth of relative dimension m−n (25.2.F(a)). (c) If π^*Ω_Y → Ω_X is injective (i.e., tangent map surjective) then π is smooth (25.2.F(b)). (d) Smoothness is preserved under base-change/cancellation in appropriate setups (25.2.G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exercises give practical checks: verify fiber smoothness or surjectivity on tangent/cotangent maps, and use induction and slicing arguments (slicing criterion for flatness/regularity). They are intended to be applied locally (on stalks) and often reduce to checking Jacobian-type rank conditions on fibers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic smoothness results (25.3.1 and 25.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If k has characteristic 0 and π:X→Y is a dominant morphism of integral k-varieties, there exists a nonempty dense open U⊂X such that π|_U is smooth of relative dimension dim X − dim Y (generic smoothness on the source). If X is smooth over k and π:X→Y is finite type, then there exists a dense open U⊂Y such that π|_{π^{-1}(U)} is smooth (generic smoothness on the target).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These theorems rely on separability in char 0 (K(X)/K(Y) separably generated) and on upper semicontinuity results for ranks of coherent sheaves and generic flatness. Lemma 25.3.4 gives a dimension bound for loci of insufficient rank; Chevalley's theorem and semicontinuity finish the argument. The results fail in positive characteristic in general (counterexamples given).
